title: Commas Written From One to N
statement:
You write every integer from 1 to n in standard notation, with a comma between each group of three digits counted from the right: 999, 1,000, 12,345, 1,000,000.

Return the total number of commas you write.

examples.why: No number below 1,000 needs a comma.
Every number from 1,000 to 12,345 has exactly one comma, and there are 12345 − 1000 + 1 of them.

hints: How many commas does a single number with d digits get?
A d-digit number gets floor((d − 1) / 3) commas. So the count depends only on the number's length.
Count by thresholds instead of numbers: every number ≥ 1,000 has at least one comma, every number ≥ 1,000,000 has a second one, and so on. Each threshold t ≤ n adds n − t + 1.

explain.intuition:
A number's commas depend only on how many digits it has: 1–3 digits get none, 4–6 digits get one, 7–9 get two. So you can count per number, but there is a neater view.

Flip the question: instead of asking each number how many commas it has, ask each comma position how many numbers reach it. The first comma appears in every number from 1,000 up, which is n − 999 numbers when n ≥ 1000. A second comma appears from 1,000,000 up, and so on. Adding these thresholds gives the answer in a handful of steps, and it keeps working if n grows to 1015.
steps: While t ≤ n: add n − t + 1 to count and multiply t by 1000.
pitfalls: Off by one at the boundary: n = 1000 writes exactly one comma, so the term is n − 1000 + 1, not n − 1000.
Counting numbers with commas instead of commas. A number like 1,234,567 contributes 2.
Starting the count of commas from the left of the number instead of the right; grouping is by threes from the last digit.

solutions.title: Count commas per number
solutions.idea: For each number, its digit count d gives floor((d − 1) / 3) commas. Add them up.

solutions.title: Count by thresholds
solutions.idea: Every number at or above 1000 has a first comma, every number at or above 10⁶ a second one, and so on. Each threshold t ≤ n contributes n − t + 1.

followups: Now n can be up to 10¹⁵. Which solution still works, and why?
Count commas for all integers in [lo, hi] instead of [1, n].
